title: Almost Every Decision Gets Challenged
gist: Roughly half of being an effective architect is people skills. Three negotiations — with stakeholders, with other architects, with developers — and the language changes that decide whether anyone collaborates with you.
minute: **Read the buzzwords.** “I needed it yesterday” means time to market. “Lightning fast” means performance. “Zero downtime” means availability. They're not literal; they're the real concern.
**Gather information before negotiating**, then move the conversation off jargon and onto numbers. Five nines is 5 min 35 sec a year — about a second a day.
**Demonstration defeats discussion.** Don't argue REST versus messaging; build both in a production-like environment and show the result.
**Give the justification before the demand.** People stop listening the moment they hear something they disagree with, so the reason has to arrive first.
**Turn requests into favours** and use people's names. Humans dislike being told what to do and generally want to help.

sections.t: “The trading system must have five nines”
sections.alt: A table of availability percentages against downtime per year and per day, with three nines highlighted
sections.sit: Parker, the SVP sponsoring the project, insists on 99.999% availability. You know that with two hours a day between global markets when no trading happens, **99.9% would meet the requirement**. Parker isn't technical, thinks they are, and does not take correction well.
opts: Explain that they're wrong about five nines.
Correct and useless. Parker doesn't respond well to correction, especially if it reads as condescending, and you have made an adversary out of the project's sponsor.
Validate the concern, then move from jargon to numbers.

*“I understand availability is very important for this system.”* Then leave the nines vernacular behind: three nines is **86 seconds of unplanned downtime a day** — a number Parker can evaluate for a global trading system.
Divide and conquer: does the *whole* system need five nines?
Sun Tzu, applied to requirements: *if his forces are united, separate them.* Narrow it to the specific areas that genuinely need it, and both the requirement and the negotiation shrink.
sections.verdict: Hold **cost and time in reserve**. Opening with *“that's going to cost a lot”* or *“we don't have time”* starts the negotiation on the wrong foot — try every other justification first, and bring money up only once you've agreed on the substance. And note where the useful information came from: the phrase *five nines* told you the concern was availability before any requirement document did.

sections.t: Addison insists REST is always faster than messaging
sections.alt: The four Cs: communicate, collaborate, clear, concise
sections.sit: You're the senior of two architects. You want asynchronous messaging between a group of services for performance and scalability. Addison strongly disagrees, citing a Google search and the output of a generative-AI prompt. This isn't your first heated debate with them.
opts: It intensifies the animosity, and an unhealthy relationship between the two architects on a project lands squarely on the development team.
Build both in a production-like environment and show the numbers.
**Demonstration defeats discussion.** Every environment differs, which is exactly why Googling it rarely yields the right answer — and why a measurement ends the argument without an argument.
sections.verdict: When a negotiation turns personal or heated, **stop it and re-engage later**, once both parties have calmed down. Architects argue; the ones who stay calm and project leadership generally find the other person backs down. This is also why the chapter treats politics as a technical skill rather than an unfortunate distraction.

sections.t: A developer wants the framework you rejected
sections.alt: Three commanding phrasings beside three collaborative rewrites
sections.sit: You chose Framework X because Framework Y doesn't satisfy the system's security requirements. A developer strongly disagrees and wants Y.
opts: Explain your analysis and move on.
You may be right, and you have spent credibility rather than earned it — and the developer still doesn't believe you.
Tell them: show me how Y addresses the security concerns and we'll use it.

**Either outcome is a win.** If they fail, they understand first-hand why Y is out, and because they reached it themselves, you have their buy-in automatically. If they succeed, you missed something and now you have a better solution — and they still feel part of the decision.
sections.verdict: This is the same principle as the phrasing changes. *“You must go through the Business layer”* invites disagreement; *“since change control is most important to us we closed the layers, which means all database calls come from Business”* puts the justification first and turns a demand into a statement of fact — and the developer's reply changes from *“I disagree”* to *“OK, but how do I handle performance on simple queries?”* Same constraint, completely different conversation.

sections.alt: A beam balanced between pragmatic and visionary
sections.cap: Both ends are failures. The balance is what earns respect from stakeholders and developers at once.
sections.p: A **visionary** plans the future with imagination and wisdom, which is what keeps an architecture vital for years — and left alone, produces solutions too theoretical to implement or understand. A **pragmatist** deals with things sensibly: budget, time, the team's actual skill level, the trade-offs of each decision, the technical limits of the design.
items: Faced with unexplained load spikes, the visionary answer is a data mesh — distributed domain-partitioned databases separating analytical from transactional concerns. Possible in theory. Has the company ever run one? What are its trade-offs? Would it even solve this?

The pragmatic first move is to **find the bottleneck**. Is the database the constraint for some of the services? Could caching reduce the calls? That is not a lesser answer; it is the answer that ships.

**Accidental complexity** is the failure mode to watch in yourself: complexity added to prove worth when something looks too simple, to stay in the loop on decisions, or for job security. *Developers are drawn to complexity like moths to a flame — frequently with the same result.*

sections.alt: Three commanding phrasings beside three collaborative rewrites
sections.cap: “No matter what the problem is, it's a people problem.” — Gerald Weinberg
items: **One sentence can close a team.** A developer suggests something, the architect says *“well, that's a dumb idea”* — and now nobody in the room offers anything again.
**“What you need to do is” → “Have you considered”.** The first is communicating without collaborating. The second returns control to the developer and starts a conversation.

**Turn a request into a favour, and use the person's name.** *“Sridhar, I'm in a real bind and I waited too long — any way you could squeeze this in?”* works where *“I'm going to need you to…”* got a flat refusal. Learn names, learn correct pronunciation, repeat it back and ask if you got it right.
**Facilitate collaboration between others, not just with yourself.** If you hear a team member using demanding or condescending language, take them aside and coach them on it.
**Become the go-to person.** Step in when someone is stuck, technically or otherwise; run periodic brown-bag sessions, which double as practice at mentoring and public speaking.
sections.p: On meetings: they arrive in two kinds — imposed on you, and imposed by you. For the first, **ask why you're needed**, and ask for the agenda; if the point is keeping you in the loop, that is what meeting notes are for. Ask whether you're needed for the whole thing or one agenda item. And when a developer or tech lead is invited, **consider going in their place** — it costs you time and it buys the team focus, and their respect. On conduct: a firm handshake with eye contact, two or three seconds, aware that greetings are cultural. Never hugs — in a professional setting they make people uncomfortable and can become harassment.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 25: Negotiation and Leadership Skills, pp. 453–472. The chapter recommends Tanya Reilly's The Staff Engineer's Path and Fisher, Ury & Patton's Getting to Yes.
